scope: Precision of the automatic `grounded_outdated` label against manual adjudication, and the corrected failure-level rate.

precision_of_automatic_label.definition: share of automatically-labelled grounded_outdated items that are genuinely superseded facts

precision_varies_by_generator: The automatic label's precision is NOT constant across generators: it is 47% on mistral_large, 30% on qwen32b, 24% on qwen3b. The echo failure mode -- an answer lifted from stale news that was never correct -- is concentrated in the smaller models; when the 123B produces a grounded-looking wrong answer it is far more often a genuinely superseded fact. Correcting every generator by one pooled precision would therefore have been wrong, and we use each generator's own audited precision where one exists.
finding: The automatic label is right about 30 of 90 sampled items (33%, 95% Wilson [24%, 44%]). The dominant error is what we call an ECHO: an answer pulled from the stale context that was never a correct answer to the question at any time (41 of 90), plus outright type errors (10) and non-answers (9). Correcting the automatic counts by this precision, faithful reporting of a superseded fact accounts for roughly 13.7-15.9-17.4% of stale-index failures, not the 37.2-53.6-56.6% the unaudited rule reports.
implication: Both modes are dangerous and both are grounded in the retrieved text, but they call for different mitigations. A faithfully-read superseded fact is a freshness problem: the fix is recency-aware retrieval or date-conditioned generation. An echo is a grounding and calibration problem: the evidence does not support the answer at all, and the fix is abstention or answer-verification. Reporting them as one number, as the unaudited taxonomy did, points at the wrong fix for the majority of failures.
